common_name: Cactus Flowered Zinnia (Twisted-Petal Heirloom Cut Flower)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil, or start indoors 4 weeks early for an earlier bloom; zinnias thrive in the heat of a Gulf Coast summer and bloom continuously until frost.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Cactus Flowered zinnia is a classic heirloom strain distinguished by long, narrow, twisted and rolled petals that curl and quill like a cactus-flowered dahlia, giving the large, four- to five-inch blooms a shaggy, dramatic texture very different from flat-petaled standard zinnias. The tall, sturdy plants bloom in a vivid mix of reds, oranges, pinks, and yellows from early summer through frost, and the unusual petal form makes them a standout in cutting gardens and mixed bouquets. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to keep the plant flowering, and water at the base rather than overhead to help avoid the powdery mildew that zinnias are prone to in humid climates.

common_name: Giant Dahlia Flowered Zinnia (Classic Large Double-Bloom Cutting Zinnia)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 4 weeks early; give tall plants sturdy support in windy sites and full sun for the biggest blooms.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after frost risk passes. Giant Dahlia Flowered is one of the oldest and best-known zinnia strains, producing fully double, densely petaled blooms up to five or six inches across that closely resemble dahlia flowers, held on tall, sturdy stems that make them outstanding for cutting. The mixed strain covers a broad range of vivid colors from crimson and scarlet through orange, pink, purple, and cream, and a single row of plants can provide a long season of bouquet material from midsummer through frost. Pinch young plants once to encourage branching and more stems, deadhead regularly to keep flowers coming, and water at the soil line rather than overhead, since wet foliage in humid weather invites powdery mildew.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or start indoors 4-6 weeks early for earlier bloom; marigolds are heat- and drought-tolerant once established, well suited to a long Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Torch is a classic French marigold named for its fiery flame-colored blooms — deep red-orange petals boldly striped and tipped with golden yellow — carried in abundance on compact, bushy, well-branched plants. It is a reliable, low-maintenance bedding and border marigold, blooming continuously from early summer to frost with minimal care, and tolerates heat and short dry spells better than most other bedding annuals. Deadhead spent flowers to keep the show going, and avoid overhead watering late in the day, since marigold foliage is prone to fungal issues if it stays wet overnight in humid weather.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in average, even lean soil in full sun; cosmos flowers best in poor to average soil, since overly rich soil produces lush foliage at the expense of blooms.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes. Seashells is a distinctive heirloom-style cosmos strain in which each petal curls and fuses into a fluted, tubular scroll, giving the airy, three-inch flowers a whimsical, seashell- or ribbon-like texture unlike any standard flat-petaled cosmos, in a soft mix of pink, white, and rose shades. The tall, wispy plants with finely divided, fern-like foliage are wind- and heat-tolerant and bloom prolifically from midsummer through frost, making excellent, long-lasting cut flowers. Deadhead regularly to extend bloom, and avoid fertilizing heavily, since cosmos naturally performs best and stays sturdiest in leaner soil; taller plantings may benefit from light staking or growing among other plants for support in open, windy sites.

common_name: Elephant Head Amaranth (Dramatic Drooping Ornamental Grain Amaranth)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil; this tall, heat-loving amaranth thrives in the long, hot Gulf Coast summer and needs a full season to develop its massive seed head.

directions: Direct sow seed a quarter-inch deep in average, well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, thinning seedlings to their final spacing since they resent transplanting once established. Elephant Head amaranth is grown for its dramatic, thick, deeply lobed, drooping seed head, which curves and folds over itself in a shape strikingly reminiscent of an elephant's trunk or head, colored in deep wine-red to maroon and reaching well over a foot long on a robust, statuesque plant. Beyond its striking presence as a garden and dried-flower accent, it is a true grain amaranth: the abundant small seeds are edible and nutritious, traditionally harvested and ground much like other grain amaranths, and the young leaves are edible as a cooked green as well. Stake in exposed, windy sites, since the heavy seed head can weigh the stalk over, and harvest for drying once the head has fully colored and the seed inside begins to feel firm.
